title: Silicon Quantum Computing Traces 25-Year Roadmap to Atomic-Precision Manufacturing in Nature Nanotechnology
excerpt: Silicon Quantum Computing (SQC) has detailed a 25-year roadmap in Nature Nanotechnology for developing atomic-scale processors. The article traces the evolution of phosphorus-in-silicon quantum processors from single-atom transistor demonstrations to commercial atomic-scale products. Key milestones include the development of automated atomic-precision fabrication, achievement of high single-qubit gate fidelities and coherence times, and the deployment of commercial analog simulators.
content:
In a Comment published in Nature Nanotechnology, Silicon Quantum Computing (SQC) Head of Quantum Engineering Ludwik Kranz and CEO Michelle Simmons trace the 25-year evolution of phosphorus-in-silicon quantum processors (the 14/15 platform) from single-atom transistor demonstrations to commercial atomic-scale products.

The perspective outlines the technological progression of atomic-precision fabrication, where scanning tunneling microscope (STM) hydrogen lithography has transitioned from a manual research tool into an automated industrial process capable of placing phosphorus atoms with 0.13-nanometer spatial accuracy at rates exceeding hundreds of thousands of qubit registers per day. By leveraging high-purity, isotopically purified silicon (28Si) and epitaxial encapsulation, the platform achieves single-qubit gate fidelities exceeding 99.99% and coherence times beyond 30 seconds.

The authors note that the remaining path to universal fault tolerance centers on industrial-scale 3D integration with foundry-built classical control electronics and cryogenic interconnects. Because electron wavefunctions in silicon extend across only a few nanometers, the platform operates with higher thermal headroom than superconducting circuits, allowing utility-scale processors with hundreds of thousands of physical qubits to operate within a single dilution refrigerator.
